Alexander Scott Mercurio, 21, of Coeur d’Alene, Idaho, was sentenced today to 18 years in prison and lifetime supervised release by U.S. District Judge David C. Nye of the District of Idaho for attempting to provide material support and resources to a designated foreign terrorist organization.

According to court records, Mercurio planned to incapacitate his father with a metal pipe and take his firearms to use in a mass casualty attack on Idaho churches in the name of ISIS. Mercurio also planned to use flame-covered weapons, explosives, knives, and a machete in the attacks. A search of his house revealed that he had butane canisters, lighters, a pair of handcuffs, a knife, and a machete, as well as several firearms belonging to his father. Days before the planned attack, Mercurio stood before an ISIS flag holding a knife and pledged his allegiance to ISIS. The FBI arrested him on April 6, 2024, one day before his planned attack. In addition to his plot to attack Idaho churches, in early 2023, he created an online repository for pro-ISIS content with the purpose of spreading the doctrine of the Islamic State.

“America’s founders wanted our Nation to be a place where the faithful of any denomination could exercise their religious beliefs freely and without fear of violence,” said Principal Deputy Assistant Attorney General for National Security M. Scott Proctor. “Alexander Scott Mercurio planned to attack that fundamental freedom by bringing death and destruction to several churches. This sentence shows that the Department of Justice will relentlessly investigate, pursue, and prosecute those who would terrorize and murder Americans for exercising their religious rights.”

“The sentencing of Mercurio today sends the clear message that where individuals intend to pursue acts of terrorism against the United States – whether in Coeur d’Alene, or any other community – they will be brought to justice,” said U.S. Attorney John C. Shirts for the District of Idaho. “Protecting our communities from terrorist activity is always the number one priority of this office and the Department of Justice. I commend the investigation by the FBI, as well as the valuable assistance provided by the Coeur d’Alene Police Department, the Kootenai County Sheriff’s Office and the Ada County Sheriff’s Office.”

“With today’s sentencing, this individual is being held accountable for pledging allegiance to ISIS and planning an attack on U.S. soil,” said Assistant Director Jarod Brown of the FBI’s Counterterrorism Division. “The FBI works tirelessly to detect and prevent acts of terrorism in order to protect the American people. We will continue to work closely with our law enforcement and Justice Department partners to make sure anyone who participates in terrorist acts faces justice.”

The case was investigated by the FBI’s Joint Terrorism Task Force with assistance from the Coeur d’Alene Police Department, the Kootenai County Sheriff’s Office and the Ada County Sheriff’s Office.

The case was prosecuted by Assistant U.S. Attorneys Heather S. Patricco and David G. Robins for the District of Idaho and Trial Attorney Matthew R. Hracho of the National Security Division’s Counterterrorism Section.

#7720. Former Cravath employee considers plea deal after insider trading charges

A former Cravath, Swaine & Moore employee who was arrested on charges of insider trading last week is reportedly considering a plea deal. (Image from Shutterstock)

A former Cravath, Swaine & Moore employee who was arrested on charges of insider trading last week is reportedly considering a plea deal.

Federal prosecutors in New York allege that Chetram Balli, who is also known as Tony Balli, 54, accessed nonpublic information through his role as a document processing specialist for Cravath and traded ahead of at least five of the law firm’s major deals.

According to Law360, a one-page form order signed Thursday by U.S. Magistrate Judge Marcia M. Henry of the Eastern District of New York reveals that federal prosecutors and Balli are engaged in plea discussions.

The order also shows that Balli’s defense counsel requested more time to focus on negotiations without the risk of not being adequately prepared for a trial, Law360 reports.

Law360 requested but did not receive comment from either party.

Balli began working for Cravath in 1989. According to prosecutors, he supported attorneys by producing legal documents and U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission filings and at times had access to confidential information.

Balli was arrested Thursday after prosecutors filed a criminal complaint against him and alleged that he made more than $70,000 in illicit profits.

#7718. Three Iranian-Backed Operatives Indicted for Their Roles in Nearly 20 Terrorist Attacks and Attempted Attacks Across Europe and the United States

An official website of the United States government

Official websites use .gov A .gov website belongs to an official government organization in the United States.

Secure .gov websites use HTTPS A lock ( Lock Locked padlock ) or https:// means you’ve safely connected to the .gov website. Share sensitive information only on official, secure websites.

Note, the release has been updated to include a quote from the National Security Division.

An eight-count superseding indictment was unsealed today charging Mohammad Baqer Saad Dawood al-Saadi, a dual Iranian-Iraqi national; Mohsen Mohajeri, an Iranian national; and Mohammad Ali al-Hassani, an Iraqi national, with terrorism-related offenses for their activities in support of Kata’ib Hizballah and Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC), two U.S. designated foreign terrorist organizations (FTOs), including their involvement in nearly 20 attacks and attempted attacks throughout Europe and the United States, and a September 2026 terrorist plot at a British Royal Air Force Base in Fairford, United Kingdom, where American armed forces were stationed.

“Anyone who plans a terrorist plot on a military base housing American servicemembers will be prosecuted by the United States government,” said Attorney General Todd Blanche. “The defendants listed in the indictment allegedly supported two foreign terrorist organizations, and al-Saadi allegedly coordinated with his co-defendants in the days leading up to the attempted terrorist plot. This Department of Justice will continue dismantling terrorist networks and protecting the American people from terrorist organizations.”

“This eight-count indictment shows the determination of Iran to commit terrorist attacks in Europe and the U.S., including one plot that was recently prevented at RAF Fairfield, a British Royal Air Force Base where American forces were stationed,” said FBI Director Kash Patel. “According to the indictment, one of the subjects is behind bars awaiting trial yet he allegedly sent coded messages to assist in future acts of violence. To date, the subjects have been allegedly involved in nearly 20 attempted attacks throughout Europe and the United States in support of Kata’ib Hizballah and Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (“IRGC”), two U.S. designated foreign terrorist organizations. This FBI will use all our resources to detect and stop such terrorist attacks as we’ve done the last 21 months – with over 1,300 terrorists disrupted and nearly 7,000 Foreign Terrorist Organization related arrests, up 1,057%. All those who threaten our homeland will get the message – justice will find you.”

“Today marks a major disruption of an alleged global terrorism conspiracy,” said Acting Principal Deputy Assistant Attorney General for National Security M. Scott Proctor. “No matter where they are in the world, the National Security Division of the Department of Justice will pursue those who target American citizens and American interests.  My thanks go out to the prosecutors and law enforcement partners for their work on this case.”

“As alleged, these defendants helped orchestrate a campaign of terror on behalf of terrorist organizations affiliated with Iran that targeted Jewish communities in Europe and the United States, and the British military base, RAF Fairford, housing American service members,” said U.S. Attorney Jamie McDonald for the Southern District of New York. “Even after one of their co-conspirators was arrested and placed in federal custody, the defendants allegedly continued coordinating terrorist activity through coded communications and a network of associates overseas. The threat presented by Iran and Iran-backed terrorist groups to America and our allies is not hypothetical — it is very real. Our Office will not stop working to address and disrupt this threat, and to prosecute those responsible.”

According to the allegations contained in the superseding indictment and other court filings: Al-Saadi, Mohsen Mohajeri, and al-Hassani allegedly conspired to commit terrorist attacks in Europe and the United States on behalf of an Iran-aligned terrorist network, which included the IRGC and Kata’ib Hizballah, both of which are FTOs. Most recently, in approximately September 2026, al-Hassani allegedly orchestrated a terrorist plot at a British Royal Air Force Base (RAF Fairford) in Fairford, United Kingdom (the “RAF Fairford Terrorist Plot”), which at the time of the attempted attack, housed U.S. military aircraft and personnel.

Al-Hassani and Mohajeri, both of whom were in Iran at the time of the RAF Fairford Terrorist Plot, allegedly relied on a network of contacts in the United Kingdom. Al-Saadi, who was imprisoned and awaiting trial on pending terrorism charges in the Southern District of New York, attempted to coordinate with al-Hassani and Mohajeri from jail by passing coded messages through third parties.

Al-Saadi, a longtime operative of the IRGC and Kata’ib Hizballah, was charged in May for working with and on behalf of the IRGC and Kata’ib Hizballah, as well as other FTOs, for his involvement in planning and promoting approximately 18 terrorist attacks in Europe; and for attempting to bomb a synagogue in New York. The picture below shows al-Saadi in front of an array of machineguns in a conference room with a map of the United States on the wall next to a list of “legitimate targets” (redacted here) identifying former and current U.S. officials.

As alleged, among the individuals with whom al-Saadi worked to facilitate and carry out the European Terrorist Attacks were Mohajeri and al-Hassani. Mohajeri is an Iranian national and operative of the IRGC who coordinated with al-Saadi and al-Hassani to carry out those terrorist attacks with the IRGC’s backing. Al-Hassani, who is originally from Iraq, used his contacts and criminal associates to carry out terrorist attacks in the United Kingdom.

The European Terrorist Attacks were carried out in the name of a purportedly new terrorist group with the pseudonym Harakat Ashab al-Yamin al-Islamiya (HAYI), which is a front for Kata’ib Hizballah and other FTOs. Of the 18 terrorist attacks in the spring of 2026 for which HAYI claimed responsibility in Europe, seven took place in the United Kingdom, the most of any European country. The attacks involved arsons, explosives, and in one instance, a near-fatal stabbing in London of two Jewish men, including a dual U.S.-British citizen.

Al-Saadi, Mohajeri, and Al-Hassani were allegedly personally involved in planning many of the European Terrorist Attacks, and al-Saadi and Mohajeri helped create and publish online propaganda videos of these attacks. For example, on or about April 6, Mohajeri and al-Hassani planned attacks while together in a room in Iraq with a map of London displayed on a computer screen. In a video of that meeting, al-Hassani told Mohajeri, “we need to get focused on London.”  An image of the video is below, with Mohajeri on the right and al-Hassani on the left. HAYI then claimed responsibility for six terrorist attacks that occurred in and around London starting approximately one week later.

On or about April 17, al-Saadi, al-Hassani, and Mohajeri allegedly directed an individual to carry out one of the European Terrorist Attacks in real time. Specifically, al-Saadi, al-Hassani, and Mohajeri, along with others, were in a room watching a FaceTime video with the individual who was carrying out the attack, which was projected onto a large screen against the background of the HAYI logo. Al-Hassani directed the perpetrators’ actions, including by instructing the individual on the other end of the call to execute the attack and directing that individual to take a lighter and “light one in your hand,” “light it,” and “throw the fourth one.” Al-Saadi recorded the attack in real time, while Mohajeri recorded al-Hassani and al-Saadi in the room as they directed the attack. A still image from Mohajeri’s recording, showing al-Saadi (circled in red) and al-Hassani (circled in green), as they directed and filmed the attack, is below.

The next day, on or about April 18, al-Hassani participated in another video call with an individual carrying out an attack on a synagogue in London, with the HAYI logo projected on the background of al-Hassani’s screen. During the video call, al-Hassani directed the individual to “light it up like a Christmas tree.” The person on the video then lit an improvised explosive device and threw it at a building. An image from the video is shown below.

In March and April — overlapping with the time that al-Saadi was co-located in Iraq with Mohajeri and al-Hassani, planning the European Terrorist Attacks — al-Saadi allegedly attempted to coordinate and carry out terrorist attacks in the United States, including by targeting a synagogue in Manhattan.

On or about May 1, following the European Terrorist Attacks, al-Saadi was arrested abroad and subsequently transferred to the custody of the United States to face prosecution. Al-Saadi has been in federal custody since his arrival in the United States. For approximately four months following al-Saadi’s arrest, there were no additional attacks attributable to al-Saadi, Mohajeri, and al-Hassani.

In August, however, al-Hassani allegedly directed and paid associates in the United Kingdom to conduct preparatory steps and arrange logistics for the RAF Fairford Terrorist Plot. On Aug. 22, al-Hassani paid one individual (Individual-1) to perform pre-operational surveillance of RAF Fairford’s perimeter and al-Hassani subsequently received videos of the area surrounding the base. In later communications with al-Hassani, Individual-1 referred to him as “Ali.”

In September, al-Hassani also tasked and paid several individuals to help him prepare for the plot, including by procuring vans and barrels of fuel, researching the purchase of chemical accelerants, including large quantities of potassium chloride, and purchasing metallic objects that could be used as explosive shrapnel. At al-Hassani’s urging, those individuals commissioned custom decals that they affixed to the vans to create the appearance that they were used by a fuel delivery business and a swimming pool supply business.

On Sept. 26, al-Hassani allegedly tasked individuals to drive three vans, some of which were later determined to contain barrels of fuel, to the RAF Fairford base. That day, al-Hassani was in frequent communication with the van drivers, helping to coordinate their movements and directing them where to drive. At least two of the three vans, while en route to the perimeter of RAF Fairford, encountered a security roadblock and were not allowed to proceed on their intended route. Al-Hassani communicated with the drivers and occupants of the vans both before and after encountering the security checkpoint. In the early morning hours of Sept. 27, law enforcement authorities in the United Kingdom recovered three white vans to which the fuel delivery business logos were affixed and arrested the occupants.

While in prison in New York awaiting trial, al-Saadi has had phone calls with his immediate family members located in Iraq. As alleged, al-Saadi used those calls to pass coded messages to Mohajeri and al-Hassani in the days leading up to the RAF Fairford Terrorist Plot.

For example, in June and July, al-Saadi allegedly spoke with his mother and sister about Mohajeri. During those calls, they referred to Mohajeri by various aliases, including “Abbas, Abu Daniel” and “Sayyid Abbas.”  Al-Saadi also told his family members that he owed money to Mohajeri and directed them to pass along messages to Mohajeri about “work,” a term al-Saadi regularly used to describe terrorist activity, including on social media posts and in discussions with Mohajeri about partnering to conduct terrorist attacks. On one of those calls, al-Saadi also asked his sister, “What are they doing about all our old work?” and asked her whether it had been cancelled or just put on pause. Al-Saadi’s sister responded that “it isn’t cancelled.”

On or about Sept. 24, al-Saadi once again spoke with his immediate family by phone. On the call, al-Saadi allegedly inquired about how al-Hassani, whom al-Saadi referred to as “Ali,” was doing. Al-Saadi’s family informed al-Saadi that “Ali” had been transferred to the “International Section.”  Al-Saadi then allegedly instructed his family to “give him [al-Hassani] money so we can do it.”  As described above, three days later, al-Hassani orchestrated the RAF Fairford Terrorist Plot.

Al-Saadi, 32, is a citizen of Iraq and Iran. Mohajeri, 48, is a citizen of Iran. Al-Hassani, 35, is a citizen of Iraq. A chart containing the names, charges, and minimum and maximum penalties for the defendants is set forth below.

The Justice Department praised the outstanding investigative work of the FBI’s New York Joint Terrorism Task Force, which consists of investigators and analysts from the FBI, the NYPD, and over 50 other federal, state, and local agencies, and the FBI Washington Field Office, Counterterrorism Division, as well as the assistance of the Department of Justice’s National Security Division, Counterterrorism Section, the Justice Department’s Office of International Affairs, U.S. Customs and Border Protection, the NYPD, the New York State Police, and the Department of State.

Assistant U.S. Attorneys Jeffrey W. Coyle, Sarah L. Kushner, David J. Robles, and Chelsea L. Scism for the Southern District of New York are prosecuting the case, with assistance from James Donnelly and Paul Casey of the National Security Division’s Counterterrorism Section.

#7716. Court appears unlikely to side with inmate in lawsuit for violation of his constitutional rights

Type to search articles, cases, and authors.

The Supreme Court on Monday appeared to side with a prison paramedic in a lawsuit brought by an inmate who contends that the paramedic’s failure to provide medical treatment violated his constitutional rights. During just over 80 minutes of oral argument in Nielsen v. Watanabe, a majority of the justices seemed poised to throw out the inmate’s lawsuit, even if it wasn’t clear whether they were ready to bar such lawsuits more broadly in the future.

The inmate, Kekai Watanabe, was seriously injured in a gang-related fight while he was in a federal detention center in Hawaii. He says that he told Francis Nielsen, a paramedic who treated him, that his pain was severe, but he received only over-the-counter pain medication and was put in solitary detention, where he remained for more than two months without seeing a specialist or going to a hospital. When Watanabe received an X-ray seven months later, it revealed that he had a fractured coccyx and that chips from the bone had penetrated the soft tissue in the area. He says that he continues to be in “tremendous pain.”

Watanabe filed a lawsuit in federal court in Honolulu, alleging that Nielsen violated his rights under the Eighth Amendment to be free of cruel and unusual punishment by being deliberately indifferent to his serious medical needs. He relied on two Supreme Court cases: the court’s 1971 decision in Bivens v. Six Unknown Named Agents of Federal Bureau of Narcotics, holding that a violation of an individual’s constitutional rights by a federal official can create a federal claim for damages; and its 1980 decision in Carlson v. Green, in which the court held that the estate of an inmate who died after having an asthma attack could bring a Bivens claim when prison officials had failed to provide adequate medical care for eight hours after the attack and did not send him to the hospital during that time.

The district court dismissed Watanabe’s claim. It held that Carlson did not apply because his claim was not sufficiently similar to the facts of that case.

The U.S. Court of Appeals for the 9th Circuit reversed. It acknowledged that the Supreme Court “has cautioned against extending Bivens remedies to new contexts,” but explained that, in its view, “Watanabe’s claim is identical to Carlson in all meaningful respects” and therefore can proceed. A deeply divided court of appeals declined to rehear the case.

Representing Nielsen, Lucas Walker told the justices on Monday that the Supreme Court “has repeatedly explained that Bivens claims are disfavored, that they strain the separation of powers, and that they cannot proceed if there is any reason to think that Congress might be better suited to weigh the costs and benefits of a damages remedy.”

But Watanabe’s “claim ... also fails under a straightforward application of this Court’s Bivens framework,” Walker continued. “There are at least three” “meaningful difference[s] between his case and Carlson.” First, Watanabe had other options besides damages – such as seeking “administrative and injunctive relief.” Second, unlike the inmate in Carlson, Watanabe did not die, which “Congress could see [as] a meaningful difference.” Third and finally, there are “special factors” at play in Watanabe’s case that were not at play in Carlson, such as the Administrative Remedy Program, a grievance process created by the Bureau of Prisons in 1979, and federal laws enacted after the decision, such as the Prison Litigation Reform Act, a 1996 law that requires prisoners to use all available internal prison appeals like the ARP before going to court.

Vivek Suri, an assistant to the U.S. solicitor general who argued on behalf of the federal government, told the justices that, in the view of the United States, there are “three ways in which this Court could resolve the case.” “First, it could apply its existing standards and recognize that Carlson is now obsolete. Second, it could ... explicitly overrule Carlson. And, third, it could distinguish Carlson on its facts.” He “respectfully urge[d]” the court to choose one of the first two options, “either of which would abrogate Carlson, fully resolve the” divisions among the courts of appeals “that it has created, and end the severe practical problems that it creates for prison administration.”

Representing Watanabe, Joshua Wesneski reiterated that “the Court’s consistent message for Bivens and Carlson over the past decade” has been “[t]his far and no further.” “‘No further,’ he said, “means we should not extend those precedents. But ‘this far’ means also that Carlson remains settled law within its core context and should not be reduced to a null set. We ask only that the Court adhere to that approach.” “Indeed,” he suggested, “to overrule Carlson now would disregard Congress’s measured judgment in this area and eliminate a crucial bulwark against the encroachment on the constitutional rights of some of society’s most vulnerable members.”

Neither Chief Justice John Roberts nor Justice Brett Kavanaugh seemed receptive to Walker’s suggestion that the court should go ahead and overrule both Bivens and Carlson.

Kavanaugh asked Walker how the court should handle the “fact ... that Congress has had 55 years since Bivens and 46 years since Carlson to do so and has not done so?” “It seems,” Kavanaugh continued, “like Congress, in fact, has left Bivens and Carlson where they stood ... and Congress has operated against that backdrop.”

Walker suggested that the Supreme Court “has not hesitated to overrule past decisions, especially those where the courts had overstepped the proper judicial role.”

In response to Walker’s assertion that overruling Bivens would “clear up the confusion and hand the accountability for all of this back to Congress, where it belongs,” Kavanaugh later asked whether “another way to provide clarity [would be] to simply say that courts should apply Bivens and Carlson but not extend them?” He compared such a scenario to what the Supreme Court has done in other areas of the law, such as with the Alien Tort Statute, “where we’ve had results or decisions under a methodology we wouldn’t use anymore, but we have not overruled the original three” causes of action under “the ATS, for example. We just haven’t extended them.”

Suri addressed this point during his time at the lectern, telling Kavanaugh that “[t]he problem ... as I see it ... is the Court’s decision” holding that “the PLRA itself gives rise to a new context,” as does “the availability of injunctive relief.” “So,” he continued, “if you’re going to honor that precedent, then this is a new context,” which would mean that “there are no viable Carlson claims anymore.”

For his part, Roberts noted that the federal government had “expressly” not asked the court to overrule Bivens, “and, of course, they have broad experience in this context. And I wonder,” he asked Walker, “if you have any insight into why or at least why shouldn’t we, on that question, defer to their expertise and experience on that question?”

Walker responded that “I think the answer is that this has been an area wrought with confusion where the lower courts have really called out for guidance.”

Roberts appeared unconvinced. “[O]n the other hand,” he countered, “it could be viewed as a cautious, incremental approach to such a fundamental question” to leave Bivens intact for now.

Several justices focused on whether, if a Carlson claim was not available, an inmate in Watanabe’s shoes would still have some remedy available to him. Justice Neil Gorsuch explored whether an inmate who was the victim of medical malpractice would still be able to obtain relief in a lawsuit against the United States (rather than the individual prison official) under Federal Tort Claims Act, a 1946 law that allows private citizens to sue the federal government for (among other things) injuries caused by a federal employee.

Gorsuch elicited from Suri that “[i]n almost all the cases that” he had “encountered, ... there is an FTCA claim brought in parallel” with the claim under Carlson – in part, Suri suggested, because the standard for prevailing is lower, qualified immunity does not apply, and “[y]ou have a defendant who’s able to pay, the United States.” Suri suggested that when an inmate does not bring both kinds of claims, it may be out of a desire to harass an individual prison official or because the inmates do not have lawyers and are instead representing themselves “and are confused about how to proceed. If this Court says there are no more Carlson claims,” he concluded, “then I think it’s more likely that they will bring FTCA claims in these cases.”

Justice Samuel Alito had a similar question, asking Suri “whether Bivens in this context provides anything ... of value that is not available based on other remedies.”

Suri responded that Carlson had rested on the idea that “the FTCA was insufficient” because it “does not provide for punitive damages.” In Bivens, he emphasized, the court faced a choice between “damages or nothing” for the plaintiff. But under the FTCA, he said, “you’re already getting damages.”

Wesneski pushed back on any suggestion that the FTCA, standing alone, would – as Kavanaugh put it – “provide some remedy in meritorious cases.” And there would be other potential problems as well, he posited: for example, he said, “we know the plaintiff in Carlson v. Green would not have had a cause of action under the FTCA” under Indiana law.

Justice Amy Coney Barrett also expressed concern about what relief an inmate in a situation like Watanabe’s would be able to obtain. She first pressed Walker on the question of whether an inmate could obtain a court order instructing a prison official to do (or to refrain from doing) something, even if he could not obtain money damages for the official’s past conduct. “I want to make sure,” she said to Walker, “that, in your position, there’s no doubt that someone in a prisoner’s position like this would be able to get injunctive relief against a federal officer.”

And she later returned to a similar topic, asking Walker to “walk me through what happens in a case where a prisoner dies as a result of medical negligence and let’s say really horrific medical negligence. What recourse,” she enquired, “does that prisoner have? Is it the FTCA?”

Walker assured Barrett that, even if Carlson were overruled, claims like the one she described would generally be allowed to go forward.

Justices Sonia Sotomayor and Ketanji Brown Jackson appeared to be the most likely to side with Watanabe. Sotomayor contended that, “in the Westfall Act, Congress looked at Bivens and explicitly reserved those constitutional claims the Court had recognized” – specifically, “Bivens itself for unlawful entry ... without probable cause into private citizens’ homes when there was malfeasance in doing so, and in Carlson itself, which was a ... medical malpractice claim.”

Walker resisted Sotomayor’s characterization, telling Sotomayor that, “respectfully, I don’t think the Court has ever gone so far as to say that the Westfall Act ratified Bivens or Carlson. But what the Court has said is that it does not provide any reason to extend those cases further.”

Jackson seemed to regard Watanabe’s case as, “with respect to all major indicia of sameness,” identical to Carlson. “We have the same kind of alleged violation as in Carlson,” she told Walker. “We have the same constitutional right brought under the same legal framework by the same kind of defendant who’s housed in the same kind of federal institution.”

By contrast, Justice Elena Kagan suggested that, at the very least, Watanabe’s case involves “factual differences.” In addition to the fact that the inmate in Carlson died, she noted that “there was a view that the prison officials had actively contributed to the injury, and ... that the prison officials knew exactly what was happening while it was happening.” “[A] different way of saying the same thing,” she added a few minutes later, “is that this looks like a pretty standard medical malpractice case, bad but standard, where the factual circumstances in Carlson look like something a good deal more than that.”

A decision in the case is expected by late June or early July.

Amy Howe is the co-founder of SCOTUSblog and its primary reporter.

#7715. Texas-Based Company Pleads Guilty to Trafficking Deadly Synthetic Opioids

An official website of the United States government

Official websites use .gov A .gov website belongs to an official government organization in the United States.

Secure .gov websites use HTTPS A lock ( Lock Locked padlock ) or https:// means you’ve safely connected to the .gov website. Share sensitive information only on official, secure websites.

A business-to-business online marketplace headquartered in Texas — eWorldTrade LLC — pleaded guilty to one count of conspiracy to distribute synthetic opioids for unlawful importation into the United States and agreed to pay a criminal fine of $1,350,000 based on its ability to pay.

“The Criminal Division will hold businesses accountable that facilitate the distribution of deadly drugs that put the lives of Americans at risk – just like we would any other drug dealer,” said Assistant Attorney General A. Tysen Duva of the Justice Department’s Criminal Division. “These incredibly dangerous, illegal synthetic opioids were manufactured abroad but brought into the U.S. because of eWorldTrade. Companies who knowingly facilitate the illicit sale of controlled substances will pay the price for the Americans they put in harm’s way.”

“Businesses that knowingly facilitate the online sale of synthetic opioids are no less dangerous than cartels and foreign terrorist organizations,” said Acting Special Agent in Charge Michael Perez of Homeland Security Investigations (HSI) Nashville. “Through close coordination with our law enforcement partners domestically and abroad, HSI will continue to identify and disrupt those networks.”

According to court documents, from March 2024 through March 2025, eWorldTrade offered registered users access to dozens of products through its website, including synthetic opioids such as fentanyl, carfentanil, and nitazenes. EWorldTrade knew that these products would reach the United States through its sales. Through its paid membership tiers, eWorldTrade offered customers easier access to premium suppliers of illegal drugs if they paid more to eWorldTrade, including to China-based sellers that openly offered and sold synthetic opioids through its website. The defendant admitted that its agents knowingly and intentionally facilitated prolific sales of these illicit controlled substances and others, including heroin and methamphetamine, from international sellers to potential buyers in the United States.

The Justice Department reached its resolution with eWorldTrade based on several factors, including the nature and seriousness of the offense. As part of the plea, eWorldTrade has agreed to enhance its compliance and internal controls and report to the Justice Department on remediation and implementation of the compliance measures throughout the term. EWorldTrade did not make a timely and voluntary disclosure of wrongdoing, but it received credit for its acceptance of responsibility and cooperation with the investigation, including collecting, analyzing, and producing voluminous information, providing timely updates on facts learned during its internal investigation, and engaging in timely remedial measures. The court will sentence eWorldTrade on Dec. 14.

The HSI Knoxville Office and the U.S. Postal Inspection Service’s Chattanooga Office investigated the case.

Trial Attorneys Jayce Born and Max J. Goldman of the Criminal Division’s Money Laundering, Narcotics and Forfeiture Section (MNF) are prosecuting the case.

MNF’s mission is to take the profit out of crime, eliminate drug cartels, and protect the U.S. financial system. MNF pursues criminal prosecutions and criminal and civil asset recovery actions involving: financial facilitators who launder profits for criminals; financial institutions and their officers and employees whose actions threaten the U.S. financial system and financial institutions; international money launderers who support transnational organized crime; and the top command and control of international drug trafficking organizations.

MNF’s Narcotic and Dangerous Drug Unit investigates and prosecutes the top command and control elements of international drug cartels, drug trafficking organizations, and related transnational criminal organizations.

Antonio Oseguera Cervantes, 67, of Michoacán, Mexico, a career drug trafficker for several Mexican cartels, was sentenced today to 270 months in prison for international drug trafficking and firearm offenses.

Wenshen Xu, 52, a Honduras-based Chinese national extradited from Guatemala, was sentenced today to 12 years in prison, five years of supervised release, and a $22 million money judgement for...

Donelfert Monterroso Vasquez, 51, a Guatemalan national, pleaded guilty today to conspiring to import more than 450 kilograms of cocaine into the United States.

#7713. Justice Alito and the tradition of a written constitution

Type to search articles, cases, and authors.

A Book Review of Samuel A. Alito Jr.’s “So Ordered: An Originalist’s View of the Constitution, the Court, and Our Country (2026)”

Justice Samuel A. Alito Jr.’s new book on the Constitution, the Supreme Court, and our nation catapults him into the same category once held by Justice Antonin Scalia as a leading public intellectual on the Supreme Court. In his book, Justice Alito shares his thoughts about such subjects as originalism, textualism in statutory interpretation, the Catholic intellectual tradition, the role of judges in the United States and increasingly around the world, religious liberty in the United States, threats to the Constitution, and much more. Although there is a great deal else to be said, several things leapt out at me.

First, it is clear that while Justice Alito is deeply attuned to precedent and Supreme Court case law, this will not get in the way of his originalism and what he sees as bad law which must be overturned. Hence his vote to overrule Roe v. Wade after 49 years, Humphrey’s Executor after 91 years, or even a 128-year-old, long settled Supreme Court precedent like United States v. Wong Kim Ark, which would have ended birthright citizenship. (In saying this, I take no position myself on the birthright citizenship case – a debate I stayed out of.)

But Justice Alito is not simply an originalist. He also rejects the view of Professor James Bradley Thayer, and of Justices Oliver Wendell Holmes, Felix Frankfurter, William H. Rehnquist, and even at times of Justice Scalia that the Supreme Court should be judicially restrained and defer blindly to the political process. Justice Alito recognizes that judicial restraint where the Supreme Court has wrongly deferred to the political process is unconstitutional under Article III and has produced tragic results in cases like Plessy v. Ferguson, in which the court ratified Jim Crow race discrimination by the political branches of the government, or Korematsu v. United States, in which the court ratified President Franklin D. Roosevelt’s internment of over 100,000 innocent Japanese American citizens. In those cases the Supreme Court erred by not enforcing the Constitution. Yet at other times it has erred by being judicially activist as in Dred Scott v. Sanford or Lochner v. New York or Roe v. Wade. As Justice Alito teaches us, the Supreme Court should be neither judicially activist nor judicially restrained. It should uphold constitutional laws and strike down unconstitutional laws. This is what the rule of law is all about.

Justice Alito is equally and rightly skeptical of the notion that judges should be Dworkinian natural rights theorists, progressive constitutionalists like Chief Justice Earl Warren, or implementers of Catholic natural law as is argued by Harvard Law School Professor Adrian Vermeule. Indeed, Justice Alito devotes a whole chapter of his book to rejecting the idea that Supreme Court justices should implement natural law. This is because Justice Alito is profoundly aware that the American people during the 237 years from 1789 to 2026 have more knowledge and are thus wiser than is one individual Supreme Court, Supreme Court justice, or academic theorist. Although he does not say this outright, Alito appears to believe that originalist judges should be guided by the four cardinal virtues: 1) practical wisdom; 2) justice; 3) courage; and 4) temperance.

At the same time, Justice Alito is very much a Burkean. What does this mean? It calls to mind one of my favorite works of political philosophy, Friedrich Hayek’s volumes 1, 2, and 3 of Law, Legislation, and Liberty. In that masterpiece, Hayek identifies two forms of social order: planned systems of order like a firm or a military platoon, and spontaneous systems of social order like a language, the free market, or a culture of following the rule of law. No one has ever successfully planned a language, but languages have rules of grammar and a fixed meaning of words, and so a language forms what Hayek calls a spontaneous system of social order.

The Constitution and its amendments are a planned system of order, the words of which are so short and abstract that they have given rise to spontaneous systems of order around them. Thus, the freedom of speech and of the press protects thoughts in a private diary or a letter to a friend even though they are not vocal utterances or made with a printing press. Those words also protect freedom of expression in new technologies like movies, radio, television, or the internet, and they even protect expressive conduct that is not vocal at all like burning the American flag contemptuously at a protest rally.

The advantage of a spontaneous system of order like a language, the free market, or constitutional caselaw is that it harnesses the wisdom of many individuals who are always wiser than is one judge or academic theorist. But the countervailing advantage of the Constitution being a planned system of order is that if constitutional case law drifts too far away from the wonderful Novus Ordo Seclorum plan of the framers, the Supreme Court may overrule such caselaw – even after a century of it having been decided. The bottom line is that in figuring out when to follow the planned order of the Constitution or the spontaneous order of constitutional case law and precedents, a justice must further draw on the four cardinal virtues mentioned earlier – practical wisdom, justice, courage, and temperance.

More controversially, Alito argues that one factor in a good constitutional or statutory interpretation is that it produces good consequences. This is contrary to what Justice Scalia used to tell me when I was his law clerk, which is that if a text he is interpreting coming in is garbage, then the decision going out will also be garbage. Justice Scalia insisted it was not his job to make the law better. This differed from the approach which Judge Robert H. Bork, who I clerked for on the D.C. Circuit, followed. Judge Bork would not rewrite the Constitution or statutes to produce good results, but if there were two equally plausible readings of legal language, Judge Bork, like Justice Alito, would go with the one that produced the best outcomes in his view. I would do the same thing.

Nevertheless, in discussing Supreme Court precedents that he thinks were wrongly decided, Justice Alito can sometimes be too timid (in my opinion) in his criticisms. Perhaps that is because as a Supreme Court justice, he feels constrained in calling for the overruling of clearly incorrect precedents. For example, he criticizes Justice Scalia’s opinion in 2012’s United States v. Jones, in which the court held evidence should be suppressed which was obtained from illegally placing a GPS tracking device on a drug dealer’s car. But in his own dissent in that case Justice Alito failed to call for overruling the exclusionary rule cases on which that decision was based, even though his former boss, Attorney General Ed Meese, had publicly called for the overruling of the exclusionary rule in the 1980’s, and even though Congress passed a federal statute overruling it in the context of Miranda v. Arizona in 1968.

Justice Alito also complains rightly about the banning of religion from the public square, but he concedes in his book that as a justice he had failed to join a Scalia dissent, which called for the complete overruling of Flast v. Cohen, an absurd standing precedent of the Warren court which gave taxpayer standing to ACLU litigants who were offended by local government Christmas and Hannukah displays or displays of the Ten Commandments. And Justice Alito quite rightly criticizes Justice Scalia’s decision weakening the free exercise clause case in Employment Division v. Smith, but he does not call for overruling it. He should do so with pride.

The argument for originalism in constitutional interpretation is the same as the argument Justice Alito makes for textualism in statutory interpretation. Legal texts, be they constitutions, statutes, contracts, wills, or Supreme Court opinions should be given their original public meaning. A judge who interpreted a Supreme Court opinion or a contract according to natural law would be violating the fundamental norms of our legal system. Originalist justices can and should follow non-originalist precedents where not doing so would be disruptive to our legal system. I thus agree with Justice Alito that the Supreme Court should follow, for example, its dormant commerce clause precedents.

There is one final area where I and Justice Alito respectfully disagree. Readers of this site, and of Justice Alito’s book, know that we have different views on same-sex marriage and Obergefell v. Hodges. In his book, Justice Alito responds to me by pointing out, among other things, that same-sex marriage was unheard of for 40,000 years of human history.

I will only add here that 250 years ago, on July 4, 1776, nearly every country in the world had slavery, feudalism was widely practiced, there was a caste system in India, racism and religious persecutions were the norm, women’s rights were suppressed, and the public was adamantly opposed to LGTBQ+ rights. Gordon Wood, the famous historian of the American Founding argued in his Pulitzer Prize winning book, The Radicalism of the American Revolution that July 4, 1776 was the most important day in all of human history (other than the days of the birth and death of Jesus) because the Declaration of Independence launched a “New Order of the Ages,” which helped bring millennia of human inequality to an end in Western democracies.

It is true that same-sex civil marriage is a very new idea, but so too, in the historical scale of things, is the end or attempted end of slavery, feudalism, the Hindu caste system, racism, religious persecution, and sexism. I think the sudden rise of same-sex marriage stems from the same American Revolution that began 250 years ago on July 4, 1776.

In any event, Justice Alito is to be commended for writing an exceptionally intellectual and provocative new book. The book fills the shoes of the late Justice Scalia, and I would recommend it to everyone – whether they agree with Justice Alito’s jurisprudence or not.

Professor Steven Gow Calabresi is the Clayton J. & Henry R. Barber Professor of Law at Northwestern Pritzker School of Law.

#7712. “Lows” Gang Member Sentenced to 10 Years in Prison For His Participation in a RICO Conspiracy

An official website of the United States government

Official websites use .gov A .gov website belongs to an official government organization in the United States.

Secure .gov websites use HTTPS A lock ( Lock Locked padlock ) or https:// means you’ve safely connected to the .gov website. Share sensitive information only on official, secure websites.

A federal judge sentenced Deontae Jackson, 37, of Minneapolis to 10 years in prison for his role in a Racketeering Influenced Corrupt Organization (RICO) conspiracy that included violence and fentanyl distribution. Jackson is the first of 14 defendants sentenced in this case, U.S. v. Alowonle et al. (24-cr-293).

According to court documents, beginning on or about 2009 and continuing through at least April 2026, Jackson was a member of and associated with the Lows gang. The Lows gang does not have a formal structure or initiation process as it is comprised of several affiliated subsets. Members would prove their loyalty by “putting in work,” which included committing acts of violence and drug trafficking.

Between February 2023 and May 2024, Jackson sold fentanyl as part of, and to benefit, the Lows gang. The Lows drug trafficking activities during this period involved over 1.2 kilograms of fentanyl.

On April 26, 2024, law enforcement searched a home in Fridley, Minnesota, where Jackson was staying. In Jackson’s bedroom, officers found approximately 945 M-30 fentanyl pills, which collectively weighed around 94.5 grams. At the time of the search, Jackson was on electronic court monitoring in connection with his conviction for a gang-related drive-by shooting. After the search, Jackson removed his ankle monitor to avoid having his location tracked.

In May 2024, law enforcement tracked Jackson to Bismarck, North Dakota. Officers then searched Jackson’s hotel room where he was staying with a fellow Lows member and two others. Police recovered a bag containing 2,599 M-30 fentanyl pills that weighed approximately 270.4 grams. In a second bag, officers found 20 more M-30 fentanyl pills that weighed 2.08 grams.

Assistant Attorney General A. Kuszynski of the IRS Criminal Investigation (IRS-CI) Chicago Field Office; Special Agent in Charge Travis Pickard of the Homeland Security Investigations (HSI) St. Paul Field Office; and Inspector in Charge Brian Musgrove of the U.S. Postal Inspection Service (USPIS) Denver Division made the announcement.

#7711. The New FBI: Better Technology to Meet the Mission

A .gov website belongs to an official government organization in the United States.

A lock () or https:// means you've safely connected to the .gov website. Share sensitive information only on official, secure websites.

Share on X X.com Share on Facebook Facebook Email Email

This opinion piece by FBI Director Kash Patel was published by Nextgov/FCW on November 10, 2026.

Of this FBI’s many historic successes over the last 21 months of the Trump administration, perhaps our most consequential has been our complete overhaul in technology capabilities. For too long, outdated technology and bureaucratic processes slowed the Bureau's ability to deliver results. Those days are over.

Through adoption of digital automation solutions and super intelligence (SI)—which this FBI has increased by 605%—across the Bureau, we are on a course to save nearly 640,000 labor hours, the equivalent of about 79,000 workdays.

Our SI program began by listening to the people doing the work. Through our SI Champions Program and Task Force, we started collecting success stories from across the field, and early results have been tremendous. In the past 90 days alone, users of our programs report saving an estimated 829 hours, about 104 workdays, by automating transcription, accelerating translation, reducing data triage, and streamlining jail call review. If that pace holds, every year these use cases alone will return more than 3,300 hours, or over 413 workdays.

These are much bigger than numbers—they are cases that matter to the American people. For example, in San Antonio, during multiple investigations of human trafficking, drug trafficking, fraud, and money laundering, one wiretap alone produced more than 1,900 sessions of poor-quality audio. SI transcription saved roughly 633 hours of manual work.

More importantly, in one specific case, the time saved allowed agents to move quickly enough to help rescue a trafficking victim and return the victim safely to their family. In another case out of Mobile, analysis of jail calls in threat cases used to take months. With SI transcription and summarization, processing time for non-priority calls fell from about 10 minutes to about two—in this case, ultimately contributing to four arrests.

Our digital automation solutions program uses software bots to handle repetitive, transaction-based computer tasks, freeing people for analytical work that requires human judgment. Twenty-nine offices across the Bureau have deployed automations.

As of October, we have fielded more than 121 of them, connected to dozens of existing FBI applications, saving over 635,000 labor hours. One specific automation helps our Human Resources Division enter benefits data for new employees, saving about 1,275 hours a year and giving new hires a more efficient transition.

Hippo Chat, the FBI’s new SI chatbot built directly into our systems, reduces administrative workload associated with file reviews and other evaluations. It synthesizes large quantities of documents, like large search warrant returns, into a readable format with the relevant information—reviewing thousands of photos at one time, organizing them into a spreadsheet for easy triage by cases agents and analysts and more.

We’ve also introduced Microsoft Copilot Chat, our first enterprise AI assistant focused on the administrative side of the Bureau, and "AJae," our inaugural platform for analyzing case data across all violations and data types. These apps free up thousands of critical hours per year for our agents and intelligence analysts in the field. None of this would be possible without our private sector partners and their cutting-edge integration to advance our mission capabilities—marking the most wide-ranging and impactful partnerships for technology in Bureau history.

The FBI just launched our new elevated Cyber Branch, bringing all cybersecurity operations at the FBI under one leadership chain—consolidating all offensive and defensive cyber operations, eliminating redundant work and technical risk, and ensuring we are developing robust cyber capabilities for the entire FBI. We’re evolving how we do business to better meet the demands of the dynamic threat landscape and provide better resources for the agents, analysts, and professional staff working hard in the field. This will greatly accelerate our work to ensure the FBI maintains the strongest cyber infrastructure in the world.

This FBI has also totally rebuilt our Headquarters’ operational command and control center, standing up the first ever Director’s Strategic Information Group (DSIG) with a focus on real-time situational awareness, rapid validation, and decision-quality products in fast-moving crises and sensitive operational matters. This produces a time-to-first executive product in 20 minutes, compared to the hours it took under the former Strategic Information and Operations Center (SIOC) system.

This is the technology that has strongly contributed to the most prolific reduction in violent crime in American history: 71,650 violent crime arrests, a 114% increase compared to the final 21 months of the previous administration; 4,616 kilograms of deadly drugs seized, up 32%, including enough fentanyl to potentially kill more than 350 million Americans; 5,801 child victims identified or located, up 25%; 6,744 arrests tied to foreign terrorist organizations, an increase of 1,057%; 10 fugitives from the FBI’s Ten Most Wanted Fugitives list arrested, including alleged murderers, rapists, and other violent criminals—2.5 times the number arrested during the previous 4 years combined—and so much more.

The principle is simple: Technology should serve the mission, allowing our people to better serve Americans. Every hour we return to our workforce is an hour for the work only they can do: crushing violent crime, defending the homeland, protecting victims, and stopping threats before they reach our communities. Mission First.

Kash Patel is the Director of the Federal Bureau of Investigation.

#7708. A White House ballroom petition and border wall backlash

Type to search articles, cases, and authors.

The Supreme Court Building is closed today for Veterans Day. In recognition of that, this is an abridged edition of SCOTUStoday.

The Trump administration has brought the battle over construction of a new White House ballroom back to the Supreme Court. In a petition for review filed last week but made public on Monday, U.S. Solicitor General D. John Sauer told the justices that the project “should be permitted to move forward outside the shadow of judicial superintendence.” For more on the petition, see the On Site section below.

On Tuesday, the justices heard argument in Department of Labor v. Sun Valley Orchards, LLC, on whether the Constitution allows the executive branch – as opposed to the courts – to adjudicate an employer’s obligation to comply with employment agreements concerning temporary immigrant workers.

On Friday, the justices will meet in a private conference to discuss cases and vote on petitions for review. Orders from Friday’s conference are expected on Monday at 9:30 a.m. EST.

Kelsey Dallas is SCOTUSblog's managing editor and the primary author of the SCOTUStoday newsletter.

#7707. Justice Department Announces Actions to Disrupt North Korea’s Massive Theft of Cryptocurrency

An official website of the United States government

Official websites use .gov A .gov website belongs to an official government organization in the United States.

Secure .gov websites use HTTPS A lock ( Lock Locked padlock ) or https:// means you’ve safely connected to the .gov website. Share sensitive information only on official, secure websites.

Today the Department of Justice announced coordinated actions against the Democratic People’s Republic of North Korea (DPRK) government’s schemes to fund its regime through the massive theft of cryptocurrency. These actions include the seizure of cloud-based infrastructure used in the FaceStealer social engineering scheme that has resulted in the theft of more than $400 million worth of cryptocurrency and the court-authorized seizure and restraint of more than $1.2 billion worth of cryptocurrency recently stolen from Binance, a virtual currency exchange.

“North Korea’s government bankrolls its rogue regime and illicit weapons program through cryptocurrency theft,” said Principal Deputy Assistant Attorney General for National Security M. Scott Proctor. “Today’s announcement shows that America will fight back against that corrupt regime’s effort to profit through cybercrime. The National Security Division will use every tool at its disposal to seize and return North Korea’s ill-gotten gains.”

“The Criminal Division, specifically the Computer Crime and Intellectual Property Section (CCIPS), and our law enforcement partners played the critical role in immediately freezing billions of dollars’ worth of stolen Binance digital assets before they got beyond law enforcement reach,” said Assistant Attorney General A. Tysen Duva of the Justice Department’s Criminal Division. “As the Department’s liaison to the digital asset industry, the Criminal Division quickly and efficiently used its expertise to immediately halt about half of this historic breach.”

“Cryptocurrency unfortunately has become fertile ground for North Korea to defraud victims and fund its malign activities,” said First Assistant U.S. Attorney Bill Essayli for the Central District of California. “Today’s seizure shows that America will continue the fight against rogue states who financially gain from cybercrime.”

“By springing into action at a moment’s notice, we worked together to freeze this massive criminal fraud in its tracks,” said U.S. Attorney Jeanine Ferris Pirro for the District of Columbia. “The North Korean regime may think they are sophisticated cyber criminals, but we have consistently met them head on, as we did here seizing more than $1.2 billion of their stolen assets.”

“The North Korean regime relies on proceeds from large-scale cryptocurrency theft to fund its illicit weapons program, stealing billions of dollars in recent years,” said FBI Cyber Branch Operations Director Brett Leatherman. “North Korean cyber actors have used the FaceStealer scheme to aggressively target individuals in the cryptocurrency and Web3 sectors through deceptive social engineering tactics, resulting in the theft of more than $400 million in the last 18 months. The FBI remains committed to identifying, disrupting, and imposing cost on North Korean actors targeting the virtual asset community.”

“North Korea’s FaceStealer is a highly effective social engineering scheme capable of deceiving even the most experienced technical and security conscious computer user” said Assistant Director in Charge Patrick Grandy of the FBI’s Los Angeles Field Office. “It exploits our trust in ubiquitous video conference platforms and valued personal relationships. If you can’t imagine a scenario where you might fall prey to it, you are not thinking creatively enough. The FBI is sounding the alarm to elevate awareness of this growing scheme, now aimed not only at crypto theft, but also the exploitation of the of the open-source software supply chain.”

Seizure of FaceStealer Infrastructure – Central District of California

Today, the U.S. Attorney’s Office for the Central District of California announced the disruption of cloud-based infrastructure used by North Korean hackers in a highly effective social engineering scheme that the FBI is calling “FaceStealer.” The scheme, which relies on surreptitiously recorded videos and artificial deepfakes, has resulted in the theft of more than $400 million in the last 18 months and the attempted compromise of individuals involved in the open-source software supply chain.

North Korean hackers known publicly by the names Sapphire Sleet, UNC1069, Dangerous Password, CryptoCore, Advanced Persistent Threat 38 (APT38), BlueNoroff, and Stardust Chollima have lured targets with invitations to video meetings delivered from accounts stolen from prior victims. Once a target joins the meeting, the hackers record the target’s webcam video and play a prerecorded video of a previous victim or victims known to the target, thereby simulating the participation of trusted contacts in the meeting to gain the target’s trust. The North Korean hackers also use super intelligence (SI) to develop deepfake videos of well-known and influential individuals often in the cryptocurrency and web3 industries that make the FaceStealer scheme even more effective. Here again, they use the deepfake videos in the meetings with targets to gain the target’s trust.

During the meeting, the hackers then introduce a fake technical error into the meeting, such as claiming that the target cannot be heard, and provide a link or prompt to fix the error. The “fix” surreptitiously installs malware on the target’s computer. With the target’s computer compromised, the hackers can steal cryptocurrency or exploit the target’s access to other computer infrastructure. In several reported cases, the hackers stole cryptocurrency and hijacked communication accounts several months to more than a year after the initial compromise. As part of the scheme the hackers also accessed the new victim’s contact lists, social media, and communications apps to target the victim’s personal and professional contacts.

The North Korean hackers target individuals working in the cryptocurrency and web3 industries. Additionally, they have increasingly targeted individuals involved in the development and maintenance of open-source software with the FaceStealer technique, attempting to gain access to their devices and the software repository accounts they control. This targeting appears calculated to enable software supply-chain attacks. Pursuant to a federal warrant, the FBI seized over 900 webcam videos of FaceStealer victims.

The FBI today published a report providing greater detail on the mechanics of the FaceStealer scheme, including best practices to protect against this scheme and steps victims can take in the event of a compromise. Additionally, the FBI created a website, www.fbi.gov/facestealer, to serve as a centralized hub for resources and information on the scheme.

The effort to disrupt the FaceStealer campaign was led by Assistant U.S. Attorney Khaldoun Shobaki for the Central District of California and the FBI’s Los Angeles Field Office.

The Department, FBI, and Law Enforcement Partners Interdict More Than a Billion Dollars Worth of Virtual Assets Stolen From Binance

Separately from the FaceStealer campaign, on or about Oct. 29, members of the North Korean military, referred to by the FBI as “TraderTraitor” stole more than $6 billion worth of virtual assets from the Binance cryptocurrency exchange. Since the theft, the National Security Division’s National Security Cyber Section, the Criminal Division’s Computer Crime and Intellectual Property Section, the U.S. Attorney’s Office for the District of Columbia, and law enforcement partners have worked closely with virtual asset service providers (VASPs) to interdict the stolen assets. Collective U.S. government and private sector efforts so far have resulted in the freeze of more than $2.7 billion, with the Department having already obtained court-authorization to seize or restrain in excess of $1.2 billion of that amount.

Efforts to trace, freeze, seize, and forfeit the stolen virtual assets are ongoing, as TraderTraitor actors continue to launder such assets through various cryptocurrency bridges, mixers, and exchanges. For example, last week, the FBI, in coordination with its law enforcement partners at the U.S. Secret Service (USSS) and the Internal Revenue Service (IRS-CI), issued a Cyber Alert attributing the theft and urging VASPs to block transactions with or derived from cryptocurrency addresses TraderTraitor actors are using to launder the stolen Binance assets.

The FBI’s Los Angeles Field Office, Cyber Division, and Virtual Asset Unit are coordinating the FBI’s efforts to recover the stolen virtual assets, working in partnership with the USSS and the IRS-CI.

#7706. California coalitions sue to block Gov. Newsom’s commutation of over 500 death row sentences

California Gov. Gavin Newsom looks on during a bill-signing event Aug. 21, 2025, in Sacramento, California. (Photo by Justin Sullivan/Getty Images)

District attorneys and victims’ families have taken their fight to the California Supreme Court over California Gov. Gavin Newsom’s plan to commute over 500 death row penalty sentences.

The Criminal Justice Legal Foundation, which represents the plaintiffs, argued Monday that the governor was required to give formal notice to district attorneys before commuting 548 death penalty sentences. The plaintiffs also challenged Newsom’s broad death penalty commutations without considering individual circumstances, beyond whether a person has more than one felony conviction. Existing law permits crime victims the opportunity to speak before a governor can commute someone.

“Gov. Newsom decided his personal views should override all those who actually participated in the process, followed and applied the law,” the plaintiffs said. “He did none of that, as he freely admits. That alone is an abuse of power that must not stand,” according to coverage by Courthouse News Service.

Newsom announced Nov. 5 the commutations of all people on death row to life in prison without parole. The governor wrote a letter that said state-sanctioned killing undermines the legal system’s foundation and counters California’s values.

Newsom, who has served two terms, declared a moratorium on all executions in 2019 and leaves office in January.

#7705. Peruvian National Sentenced in Transnational Government Imposter Scheme that Defrauded Thousands of U.S. Consumers

An official website of the United States government

Official websites use .gov A .gov website belongs to an official government organization in the United States.

Secure .gov websites use HTTPS A lock ( Lock Locked padlock ) or https:// means you’ve safely connected to the .gov website. Share sensitive information only on official, secure websites.

Carla Magaly Alcedo Mendoza (Alcedo), 45, of Lima, Peru, was sentenced today to eight years in prison and three years of supervised release for overseeing a years-long transnational fraud conspiracy that used government impersonation tactics to defraud thousands of consumers across the United States.

“The Justice Department is protecting U.S. consumers from fraudsters no matter where those fraudsters operate,” said Assistant Attorney General A. Tysen Duva of the Justice Department’s Criminal Division. “We will continue to work with our partners at home and abroad to ensure that those who impersonate U.S. government and court officials to steal from Americans are brought to justice.”

“These criminals preyed on hardworking Americans, using fear and intimidation to steal millions of dollars. They deliberately targeted Spanish-speaking communities, impersonating government officials and threatening innocent people with arrest and legal consequences,” said Acting U.S. Attorney Yara Lorenzo Klukas for the Southern District of Florida. “Today's sentence sends a clear message: no matter where you operate, if you target Americans, we will pursue you and bring you to justice.”

“Today’s sentencing of the fourteenth defendant charged in this investigation was made possible by the outstanding collaboration between Miami Division Postal Inspectors, the Justice Department, and our international partners,” said Inspector in Charge Bladismir Rojo of the U.S. Postal Inspection Service (USPIS) Miami Division. “Transnational criminal organizations who victimize our citizens are not beyond our reach.”

According to court documents, Alcedo was the operator of a Peruvian call center that defrauded and extorted U.S. residents by falsely threatening them with arrest, court proceedings, and immigration consequences. Alcedo admitted that she owned and operated a call center in Lima, Peru, that placed unsolicited calls to Spanish-speaking consumers in the United States and falsely claimed that they had won or qualified for free products, including computer tablets and English language courses. On later calls, Alcedo and her co-conspirators falsely claimed that victims were contractually obligated to pay large sums of money to receive the products. Alcedo and her co-conspirators impersonated government officials and lawyers to intimidate victims and force them to pay. Alcedo and her co-conspirators also threatened victims with court proceedings, arrest, and other legal consequences if they did not pay. The scheme spanned several years and thousands of victims made payments to Alcedo. Collectively, the scheme was responsible for defrauding more than 30,000 Spanish-speaking residents of the United States out of $15 million.

Alcedo was extradited from Peru in April 2025 and pleaded guilty to conspiracy to commit mail and wire fraud in August 2026.

Including today’s sentencing in the U.S. District Court for the Southern District of Florida, 14 defendants have now been convicted and sentenced in connection with this scheme. The 14 defendants include 10 Peruvian call center owner-operators and four distribution center owner-operators who processed payments, distributed products, and facilitated the fraud in the United States, and a telephone service provider who facilitated the fraud schemes across the call centers in Peru. Alcedo and many of the defendants shared strategies on how to defraud consumer victims across the United States.

Alcedo is the 10th defendant charged in this scheme to be extradited from Peru and sentenced in federal court. In 2021 and 2022, Henrry Milla, Carlos Espinoza, Jerson Renteria, Fernan Huerta, Omar Cuzcano, Evelyng Milla, and Josmell Espinoza received sentences ranging from 88 months to 110 months in prison. In 2024, Jose Alejandro Zuñiga Cano was sentenced to 98 months in prison.

Criminal Division Senior Trial Attorney and Transnational Criminal Litigation Coordinator Phil Toomajian prosecuted the case and Assistant U.S. Attorney Annika Miranda for the Southern District of Florida is handling asset forfeiture. The Justice Department’s Office of International Affairs, U.S. Attorney’s Office for the Southern District of Florida, State Department’s Diplomatic Security Service, U.S. Marshals Service, Peruvian National Prosecutor General’s Office, and Peruvian National Police provided critical assistance with the case and extradition.

This case is part of efforts being undertaken by the Department of Justice Criminal Division’s Cyber-Enabled Scam Initiative (CSI). The CSI is a dedicated team of prosecutors built to find scammers who prey on Americans, disrupt their networks, and hold them accountable. CSI brings together expert prosecutors from across the Criminal Division to accelerate the prosecution of cyber-enabled financial crimes, including complex frauds, government imposter schemes, romance and inheritance scams, financially motivated sextortion, lottery and sweepstakes scams, and other predatory schemes. With nationwide jurisdiction and global reach, CSI leverages every available tool to dismantle criminal operations, pursue bad actors, recover criminal proceeds, and obtain justice for victims. The Criminal Division partners with U.S. Attorneys’ Offices across the country and is a founding member of the Scam Center Strike Force.
